26 A wave has a frequency of 5 GHz.
What is the period of the wave?
A
200 ps
B
2 ns
C
20 ns
D
20 000 s

hints: Notice the frequency is $5 \text{ GHz} = 5 \times 10^9 \text{ Hz}$, so first write it in standard $\text{Hz}$.
Recall period and frequency are reciprocals with $T = 1/f$, so a gigahertz frequency must give a period much smaller than $1 \text{ ns}$.
Calculate $1/(5 \times 10^9)$ in seconds, then convert seconds to picoseconds using $1 \text{ ps} = 10^{-12} \text{ s}$.
walkthrough: Identify the given quantity: frequency $f = 5 \text{ GHz} = 5 \times 10^9 \text{ Hz}$.
State the governing relation for any progressive wave: period $T = 1/f$.
Substitute the value with units: $T = 1/(5 \times 10^9 \text{ Hz})$.
Calculate the intermediate result: $T = 0.2 \times 10^{-9} \text{ s} = 2.0 \times 10^{-10} \text{ s}$.
Convert to the units used in the options using $1 \text{ ps} = 10^{-12} \text{ s}$: $T = (2.0 \times 10^{-10})/(10^{-12}) \text{ ps} = 200 \text{ ps}$.
Check the unit and size: seconds divided correctly gives a sub-nanosecond period, as expected for gigahertz waves. This is option A.

A.explanation: Period is $2.0 \times 10^{-10} \text{ s} = 200 \times 10^{-12} \text{ s}$, which is $200 \text{ ps}$.

B.explanation: This is 10 times too large and comes from a power-of-ten error when converting $2.0 \times 10^{-10} \text{ s}$ to nanoseconds.

C.explanation: This is 100 times too large and comes from treating $5 \text{ GHz}$ as $5 \text{ MHz}$ in $T = 1/f$.

D.explanation: This equals $0.02 \text{ s}$, which is far too large for a gigahertz frequency with a sub-nanosecond period.
